about: Sourced life stories for Moses, Joshua, the judges and the kings of the united kingdom. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossiers Research/People/rulers-judges.md and Research/People/rulers-united-kingdom.md.

moses-exo-2-10.short: A Levite child saved from the river, raised as Pharaoh's daughter's son, who met God at the bush and led Israel to the edge of the promised land.

paragraphs.text: Moses was born in Egypt after Pharaoh had ordered that every son born should be cast into the river. His parents were Levites; later lists name them Amram and Jochebed, with Aaron and Miriam as his brother and sister. His mother hid him for three months, then laid him in a basket of bulrushes among the reeds while his sister watched. Pharaoh's daughter found him, and his sister fetched their mother, who was paid to nurse him. When the child grew, he became Pharaoh's daughter's son, and she named him Moses: "Because I drew him out of the water."

The book of Acts says Moses "was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians". When he was grown, forty years old by Acts' count, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and killed the Egyptian. The next day a Hebrew asked him, "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" Pharaoh heard of it and sought to kill him, and Moses fled to Midian. There he helped the seven daughters of the priest Reuel at a well, married one of them, Zipporah, and named their son Gershom: "I have been a stranger in a strange land."

Forty years later, Acts says, while he was keeping the flock of his father-in-law Jethro near Horeb, Moses saw a bush that burned but was not consumed. God spoke to him from it and sent him to bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses held back, saying he was "slow of speech", and God gave him Aaron to speak for him. On the road back to Egypt the LORD met Moses and sought to kill him, and Zipporah circumcised their son. Moses was eighty when he and Aaron stood before Pharaoh.

The forty years in which he led Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness are told on his page as a leader. Exodus says that "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend." When he came down from Sinai with the tablets, the skin of his face shone and he did not know it, and the people were afraid to come near him. When Israel made the golden calf, he broke the tablets, and then pleaded for the people, asking to be blotted out of God's book if they could not be forgiven.

Jethro brought Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to Moses in the wilderness at the mount of God. Later Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman he had married, and asked whether the LORD had spoken only by him. The text adds that "the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth." When Miriam was struck with leprosy, Moses cried, "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee." Chronicles says his sons were counted with the tribe of Levi.

At Meribah, told to speak to the rock, Moses struck it twice with his rod, and God told him he would not bring the people into the land. Miriam died at Kadesh and Aaron on mount Hor. Moses begged to cross the Jordan and was told, "Let it suffice thee". From the top of Pisgah he saw the land, and he died in Moab at a hundred and twenty, "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated"; no one knows where his grave is. Israel wept for him thirty days, and Matthew tells that Moses appeared with Elias, talking with Jesus on the mountain.

joshua-exo-17-9.short: Son of Nun of Ephraim, Moses' young servant and one of two spies who urged Israel to enter the land, and later the man who led them in.

paragraphs.text: Joshua was the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim. His name at first was Oshea, and Moses called him Jehoshua. He first appears leading Israel's fighting men against Amalek at Rephidim, while Moses held up his hands on the hill.

He was Moses' "minister" and went with him up the mount of God. The text calls him "a young man" who "departed not out of the tabernacle". When two men prophesied in the camp, Joshua said, "My lord Moses, forbid them", and Moses answered, "Enviest thou for my sake?"

Joshua was one of the twelve men sent to search out Canaan. When the people wanted to turn back to Egypt, he and Caleb tore their clothes and said, "If the LORD delight in us, then he will bring us into this land". The people spoke of stoning them, but of that generation only Joshua and Caleb were promised that they would enter the land.

When Moses asked God for a man to lead the people, God named Joshua, "a man in whom is the spirit", and Moses laid his hands on him. After Moses died, Joshua led Israel over the Jordan; those years are told on his page as a leader. Near Jericho a man with a drawn sword met him as captain of the LORD's host, and Joshua fell on his face and loosed his shoe.

In old age Joshua asked for the town of Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim, built it and lived there. At Shechem he called the tribes to choose whom they would serve: "but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." He died at a hundred and ten and was buried at Timnath-serah, and Israel served the LORD all his days. Scripture names no wife or children for him.

othniel-jos-15-17.short: The first deliverer in Judges: he took Kirjath-sepher to win Caleb's daughter Achsah, then freed Israel from Chushan-rishathaim.

paragraphs.text: Othniel belonged to Caleb's family. Caleb promised his daughter Achsah to the man who took the city of Kirjath-sepher, and Othniel took it and married her. Joshua calls him "the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb"; Judges calls him "Caleb's younger brother". Chronicles lists him among the sons of Kenaz and names his son Hathath.
Achsah urged Othniel to ask her father for a field. She then asked Caleb herself for springs of water, and he gave her the upper springs and the nether springs.

After Israel had served Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years, the LORD raised up Othniel. "The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war", and he won. The land had rest forty years, and then Othniel died. His time as judge is set out on his page as a ruler.

ehud-jdg-3-15.short: A left-handed Benjamite who brought Moab's tribute to King Eglon, killed him with a hidden dagger, and led Israel to victory.

paragraphs.text: Ehud was "the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded". Israel had served Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years when the LORD raised Ehud up as a deliverer. The people sent their present to Eglon by him.

Ehud made a two-edged dagger a cubit long and hid it on his right thigh. After the present was delivered, he came back alone to the king, who was sitting in his summer parlour, and said, "I have a message from God unto thee." He drove the dagger into Eglon, locked the doors and escaped while the servants waited outside.

In mount Ephraim he blew a trumpet and told Israel, "Follow after me: for the LORD hath delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand." They held the fords of the Jordan, and about ten thousand Moabites fell. The land had rest eighty years. Beyond his father's name Scripture tells nothing of his family, and of his death only the words "when Ehud was dead".

deborah-jdg-4-4.short: A prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, who judged Israel under a palm tree in mount Ephraim and sent Barak to battle against Sisera.

paragraphs.text: Deborah was "a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth", and "she judged Israel at that time". She sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Beth-el in mount Ephraim, and the people came up to her for judgment. For twenty years Jabin, king of Canaan, and his captain Sisera had pressed Israel hard.

She sent for Barak and gave him the LORD's command to gather ten thousand men at mount Tabor. Barak said, "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go". Deborah went, telling him that the LORD would sell Sisera "into the hand of a woman". On the day of battle she told him, "Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand."

Sisera's army was routed, and he was killed in the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. Deborah and Barak sang a song of the victory, in which she says, "I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel." The land had rest forty years. Scripture does not give her tribe, any children, or her death.

gideon-jdg-6-11.short: A son of Joash of Manasseh, called while threshing in hiding, who broke Midian with three hundred men, refused to be king, and had seventy sons.

paragraphs.text: Gideon was the son of Joash the Abiezrite, of Ophrah in Manasseh. Midian had raided Israel's harvests for seven years, and Gideon was threshing wheat by the winepress to hide it from them when the angel of the LORD came to him: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Gideon answered, "my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." Fire from the rock consumed his offering, and he built an altar there.

That night, with ten of his servants, he threw down his father's altar of Baal. He did it by night "because he feared his father's household, and the men of the city". When the men of the city wanted him killed, his father Joash said, "if he be a god, let him plead for himself", and called Gideon Jerubbaal. Gideon then asked God for the sign of the fleece, wet and then dry.

With three hundred men, trumpets and lamps in pitchers, he routed the camp of Midian. He took the kings Zebah and Zalmunna, who had killed his brothers at Tabor, "the sons of my mother". He told his firstborn son Jether to kill them, but the youth was afraid, so Gideon killed them himself. The war is told more fully on his page as a ruler.

Israel asked him to rule over them, with his son and grandson after him. He answered, "I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you." But from the gold of the spoil he made an ephod and put it in Ophrah, and it "became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house".

Gideon had many wives and seventy sons, and a concubine in Shechem bore him Abimelech. He "died in a good old age" and was buried in his father's tomb at Ophrah. After his death Abimelech killed his seventy brothers "upon one stone"; only Jotham, the youngest, escaped.

tola-jdg-10-1.short: A man of Issachar who rose to defend Israel after Abimelech and judged it twenty-three years; two verses are all Scripture tells of him.

paragraphs.text: Two verses are all that Scripture tells of Tola. He was "the son of Puah, the son of Dodo, a man of Issachar", and he lived in Shamir in mount Ephraim. After Abimelech he "arose to defend Israel". He judged Israel twenty-three years, died, and was buried in Shamir.
Genesis names a Tola and a Phuvah among the sons of Issachar. Nothing is said of Tola's wars, his wife or his children.

jair-jdg-10-3.short: A Gileadite who judged Israel twenty-two years; his thirty sons rode thirty ass colts and held thirty cities.

paragraphs.text: Scripture gives Jair three verses. He was a Gileadite and judged Israel twenty-two years after Tola. "He had thirty sons that rode on thirty ass colts, and they had thirty cities, which are called Havoth-jair unto this day." He died and was buried in Camon.
Numbers gives the same name, Havoth-jair, to towns taken in Moses' time by "Jair the son of Manasseh"; Scripture does not say how the two are connected. Nothing more is told of the judge's life.

jephthah-jdg-11-1.short: A Gileadite driven from home by his half-brothers, called back to lead Gilead against Ammon, whose vow fell on his only child.

paragraphs.text: Jephthah the Gileadite was "a mighty man of valour", the son of Gilead by a harlot. His father's wife bore other sons, and when they grew up they drove him out: "Thou shalt not inherit in our father's house; for thou art the son of a strange woman." He fled to the land of Tob, where "vain men" gathered to him.

When Ammon made war on Israel, the elders of Gilead came to fetch him. He asked them, "Did not ye hate me, and expel me out of my father's house?" They promised to make him their head, and at Mizpeh the people made him head and captain over them. His dealings with the king of Ammon and the war are told on his page as a ruler.

The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he vowed that if the LORD gave him victory, whatever came out of his house to meet him on his return would be the LORD's, offered as a burnt offering. He won, and his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and dances. "She was his only child; beside her he had neither son nor daughter." He tore his clothes and cried, "Alas, my daughter!"

She told him to do as he had vowed, and asked for two months to bewail her virginity on the mountains with her friends. Then he "did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man." Scripture does not name her or say more of what was done; his page as a ruler sets out how the verse has been read. Each year the daughters of Israel went to lament her four days.

Later the men of Ephraim threatened to burn his house over him, and Gilead fought them at the fords of the Jordan, where those who said "Sibboleth" were killed. Jephthah judged Israel six years, died, and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead. Hebrews names him among those who acted by faith.

ibzan-jdg-12-8.short: A judge from Beth-lehem who judged Israel seven years; Scripture records his sixty children and his burial, and little more.

paragraphs.text: Three verses tell all that is known of Ibzan. He was "of Beth-lehem" and judged Israel seven years after Jephthah. He had thirty sons and thirty daughters; he sent his daughters out to marry and brought in thirty daughters from outside for his sons. He died and was buried at Beth-lehem, and Scripture does not say which Beth-lehem it was, or name his tribe, his wife or any deed of his.

elon-jdg-12-11.short: A man of Zebulun who judged Israel ten years and was buried in Aijalon; nothing else is recorded of him.

paragraphs.text: Two verses are all that Scripture gives Elon. He was "a Zebulonite", he judged Israel ten years after Ibzan, and he died and was buried "in Aijalon in the country of Zebulun". No family, deeds or words of his are recorded. One of Zebulun's own sons in Genesis bore the same name.

abdon-jdg-12-13.short: A Pirathonite, son of Hillel, who judged Israel eight years; his forty sons and thirty nephews rode seventy ass colts.

paragraphs.text: Three verses tell of Abdon. He was "the son of Hillel, a Pirathonite", and judged Israel eight years after Elon. "He had forty sons and thirty nephews, that rode on threescore and ten ass colts". He died and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, "in the mount of the Amalekites". Nothing else is told of him.

samson-jdg-13-24.short: A Nazarite from birth, of the tribe of Dan, whose great strength was turned against the Philistines and who died pulling down Dagon's house.

paragraphs.text: Samson's father was Manoah, a Danite of Zorah, and his mother had borne no children. The angel of the LORD told her she would have a son: no razor was to touch his head, for he would be "a Nazarite unto God from the womb", and he would "begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines". When Manoah offered a sacrifice, the angel went up in the flame of the altar. The boy was named Samson; "the child grew, and the LORD blessed him."

He wanted to marry a Philistine woman of Timnath, and when his parents asked, "Is there never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren", he said, "Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well." The text says this "was of the LORD", who sought an occasion against the Philistines. On the way he tore a young lion apart with his bare hands. At the wedding feast his riddle was found out through his wife, and he killed thirty men of Ashkelon to pay the wager. His wife was then given to his companion.

When he found his wife given to another, he set three hundred foxes with firebrands loose in the Philistines' corn, and the Philistines burned his wife and her father. Men of Judah bound him and handed him over, but the cords melted from his arms and he killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass. He judged Israel twenty years "in the days of the Philistines".

At Gaza he went in to a harlot, and at midnight carried off the doors of the city gate. Then he loved Delilah, a woman in the valley of Sorek, and the lords of the Philistines paid her to find the secret of his strength. After many days of her pressing he told her, and she had his seven locks shaved while he slept: "he wist not that the LORD was departed from him." The Philistines put out his eyes and set him grinding in the prison at Gaza, but his hair began to grow again.

At a great feast to their god Dagon, the Philistines brought Samson out to make sport for them. He prayed, "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once", and pulled down the two middle pillars. The house fell on the lords and the people, and "the dead which he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life." His brothers buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in his father's tomb.

eli-1sa-1-3.short: The aged priest at Shiloh who blessed Hannah, took in the boy Samuel, did not restrain his sons, and died when the ark was taken.

paragraphs.text: Eli was the priest at Shiloh, where his sons Hophni and Phinehas were also priests. He sat on a seat by a post of the temple of the LORD. Seeing Hannah praying silently, he took her for drunk, but when she explained, he said, "Go in peace: and the God of Israel grant thee thy petition". When her son Samuel was weaned, she brought him to Eli, and the boy served the LORD under him.

Eli's sons "were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD". They took the people's offerings by force and lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle. Eli, now very old, asked them, "Why do ye such things?", but they did not listen. A man of God told Eli that he honoured his sons above the LORD, and that both sons would die on one day.

When the LORD called the boy Samuel by night, Eli understood it and taught him to answer, "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." The word that came was against Eli's house, because "his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not". Eli asked Samuel to hide nothing, and when he had heard it, said, "It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good."

Eli was ninety-eight and his eyes were dim when Israel took the ark into battle against the Philistines. He sat by the wayside watching, for "his heart trembled for the ark of God". When a runner brought word that his sons were dead and the ark was taken, Eli fell backward from his seat at the mention of the ark, broke his neck and died, "for he was an old man, and heavy". He had judged Israel forty years. As she was dying in childbirth, his daughter-in-law named her son I-chabod.

samuel-1sa-1-20.short: The son Hannah asked of the LORD, given to the LORD at Shiloh, who grew up a prophet, judged Israel all his life, and anointed its first two kings.

paragraphs.text: Samuel's father was Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim in mount Ephraim, called "an Ephrathite". Elkanah had two wives, Peninnah, who had children, and Hannah, who had none. Year after year at Shiloh Hannah wept, and at last she vowed that if the LORD gave her a son, she would give him to the LORD all the days of his life. She bore a son and named him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD." Chronicles traces a "Shemuel, the son of Elkanah, the son of Jeroham" back to Levi.

When the child was weaned, Hannah brought him to Eli at Shiloh: "I have lent him to the LORD". The boy served before the LORD wearing a linen ephod, and every year his mother made him a little coat and brought it when she came up to sacrifice. Hannah later had three more sons and two daughters. "The child Samuel grew on, and was in favour both with the LORD, and also with men."

One night, when "the word of the LORD was precious in those days", the LORD called Samuel by name. Three times he ran to Eli, thinking Eli had called. The fourth time he answered, "Speak; for thy servant heareth." The message was judgment on Eli's house; Samuel was afraid to tell it, but told it all. "The LORD was with him, and did let none of his words fall to the ground", and all Israel knew he was a prophet.

Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life, going each year to Beth-el, Gilgal and Mizpeh and coming home to Ramah, where he built an altar. That work is told on his page as a ruler. In old age he made his sons Joel and Abiah judges, but they "took bribes, and perverted judgment", and the elders asked for a king. "The thing displeased Samuel", yet he anointed Saul at the LORD's word.

At his farewell he asked the people, "whose ox have I taken?", and they said he had wronged no one. He promised, "God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you". When Saul disobeyed, Samuel told him the LORD had rejected him, and afterwards "mourned for Saul". Sent to Bethlehem, he anointed Jesse's youngest son, David.

Samuel died, "and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him, and buried him in his house at Ramah." Later, at Endor, Saul had a woman call him up, and the text tells of Samuel saying to him, "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me". The Psalms name him "among them that call upon his name", and Jeremiah sets him beside Moses as one who stood before the LORD.

saul-1sa-9-2.short: A tall young Benjamite, son of Kish, anointed as Israel's first king, who lost God's favour, turned against David, and died on mount Gilboa.

paragraphs.text: Saul was the son of Kish, a Benjamite, "a choice young man, and a goodly"; "from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people." Sent out to look for his father's lost asses, he came to the prophet Samuel, who anointed him with oil. On the way home the Spirit of God came on him and he prophesied, and people asked, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" When the lot fell on him at Mizpeh, he was found hiding among the baggage.

His wife was Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz. Samuel's book names his sons Jonathan, Ishui and Melchi-shua and his daughters Merab and Michal; Chronicles names Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Esh-baal. The captain of his army was "Abner, the son of Ner, Saul's uncle". By his concubine Rizpah he had two more sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.

After he rescued Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites, the people made him king at Gilgal. His reign is told on his page as a ruler. Twice Samuel rebuked him for not keeping the LORD's command: once for offering the burnt offering himself, and once for sparing Agag and the best of Amalek's flocks. "To obey is better than sacrifice", Samuel told him, and the LORD rejected him as king.

Then "the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul", and an evil spirit troubled him; David played the harp to bring him relief. When the women sang, "Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands", Saul was angry and "eyed David from that day". He threw his javelin at David, gave him his daughter Michal, and then hunted him. Once, when David spared his life in a cave, Saul wept and said, "Thou art more righteous than I".

With Samuel dead and the Philistines gathered against him, Saul asked the LORD and got no answer, so he went to a woman at Endor who had a familiar spirit. In the battle on mount Gilboa his sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Melchi-shua were killed, and Saul, badly wounded, fell on a sword. The men of Jabesh-gilead took his body from the wall of Beth-shan and buried his bones. David lamented: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided". Chronicles says Saul died "for his transgression which he committed against the LORD".

ish-bosheth-2sa-2-8.short: Saul's son, made king over Israel by Abner for two years while Judah followed David, and murdered in his bed by two of his captains.

paragraphs.text: Scripture tells little of Ish-bosheth, nearly all of it in 2 Samuel 2 to 4. He was Saul's son. After Saul's death, Abner, the captain of Saul's army, brought him to Mahanaim and made him king over Gilead, Ephraim, Benjamin and "all Israel". He was forty and reigned two years, "But the house of Judah followed David." Chronicles lists a son of Saul named Esh-baal, and the site's record treats them as the same man.

When Ish-bosheth accused Abner over Rizpah, Saul's concubine, Abner turned to David, and Ish-bosheth "could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him." At David's demand he took Saul's daughter Michal from her husband and sent her back to David. When he heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, "his hands were feeble".

Two of his captains, Rechab and Baanah, came into his house at noon while he lay on his bed, killed him, and carried his head to David at Hebron. David called him "a righteous person", had the killers put to death, and buried the head in Abner's tomb in Hebron. Scripture does not name his mother, his wife or any children.

david-rut-4-17.short: The youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, a shepherd anointed by Samuel, who killed Goliath, fled from Saul, reigned forty years, and was called "the sweet psalmist of Israel".

paragraphs.text: David was the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite of Beth-lehem-judah, and great-grandson of Boaz and Ruth. Samuel says Jesse had eight sons and that David was the youngest; Chronicles names seven, with David the seventh, and gives him two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail. Scripture never names his mother. He was keeping the sheep when Samuel came and anointed him among his brothers: "he was ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance", and from that day the Spirit of the LORD came upon him.

He came to Saul's court as a harp player and armourbearer. Sent to bring food to his brothers in the army, he went out against the Philistine champion Goliath "in the name of the LORD of hosts" and killed him with a sling and a stone. Saul's son Jonathan "loved him as his own soul", and the two made a covenant. David married Saul's daughter Michal, and when Saul sent men to kill him, she let him down through a window.

Then he lived as a fugitive from Saul. At the cave of Adullam his brothers and his father's house joined him, with about four hundred men, and he left his father and mother with the king of Moab. Twice he had Saul in his power and would not harm "the LORD's anointed". He married Abigail, the widow of Nabal, and Ahinoam of Jezreel, while Saul gave Michal to another man. When Saul and Jonathan died, he lamented, "How are the mighty fallen!"

David was thirty when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years; the reign is told on his page as a ruler. When the ark came into Jerusalem he danced before the LORD with all his might, and Michal despised him; she had no child to the day of her death. He sought out Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth and had him eat at the king's table. Sons were born to him at Hebron and at Jerusalem.

He took Bath-sheba, the wife of Uriah, and had Uriah killed in battle. The prophet Nathan told him, "Thou art the man", and David said, "I have sinned against the LORD." Their first child died; their next son was Solomon. Trouble followed in his house: his son Amnon forced Absalom's sister Tamar, Absalom had Amnon killed, and later Absalom rose against his father and was killed in the battle that followed. David wept, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee".

In old age, "old and stricken in years", David named Solomon king when Adonijah tried to take the throne. He charged Solomon, "be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man", then died and was buried in the city of David. His last words call him "the sweet psalmist of Israel". Chronicles says he "died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour", and Acts recalls God's words about him: "a man after mine own heart".

solomon-2sa-5-14.short: David and Bath-sheba's son, loved by the LORD, who asked for wisdom, built the temple, and in old age was turned aside by his many wives.

paragraphs.text: Solomon was the son of David and Bath-sheba, born after their first child died. "The LORD loved him", and through the prophet Nathan he was given a second name, Jedidiah. Chronicles calls his mother Bath-shua the daughter of Ammiel, and records God's promise to David of a son who would be "a man of rest".

When his half-brother Adonijah tried to make himself king in David's old age, Nathan and Bath-sheba went to David, and Solomon was anointed at Gihon. Chronicles adds that he was made king "the second time" before all the people. He married Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David. His reign is told on his page as a ruler.

At Gibeon the LORD appeared to him in a dream and said, "Ask what I shall give thee." Solomon asked for "an understanding heart" to judge the people, and God gave him wisdom, and riches and honour besides. He judged between two women who both claimed one baby. He spoke three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, and spoke of trees, beasts, birds, creeping things and fishes.

He built the house of the LORD in seven years and his own house in thirteen. The queen of Sheba came to test him with hard questions and said, "the half was not told me". Two of his daughters, Taphath and Basmath, married officers of his kingdom.

Solomon "loved many strange women": he had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and "when Solomon was old" they turned his heart after other gods. He built high places for Chemosh and Molech, and the LORD said he would tear the kingdom from his son, but not in Solomon's days, for David's sake. After forty years as king he died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam, whose mother was Naamah an Ammonitess, reigned after him. Jesus later spoke of "Solomon in all his glory".
